title: Pectoralis major
summary: The large fan-shaped chest muscle that pulls the arm across the body.

layers.basics: This chest muscle swings your arm forward and inward, as when you push or hug.
layers.deeper: It runs from the collarbone, sternum and rib cartilages to the upper humerus. It adducts and medially rotates the arm and helps in pushing.
layers.expert: Innervated by the medial and lateral pectoral nerves (C5-T1); clavicular head flexes the shoulder, sternocostal head extends it from a flexed position.

did_you_know: In women the breast sits on top of this muscle; it is not itself breast tissue.

title: Deltoid
summary: The rounded shoulder muscle that lifts the arm.

layers.basics: The cap of your shoulder; it raises your arm out to the side, forward and back.
layers.deeper: Three parts (anterior, middle, posterior) act together to abduct the arm and individually to flex or extend it.
layers.expert: Axillary nerve (C5-C6). Middle fibers are multipennate, giving force for abduction beyond the first ~15° initiated by supraspinatus.

did_you_know: Deltoid injections are common because the muscle is thick and accessible.

title: Biceps brachii
summary: The two-headed front-of-arm muscle that bends the elbow and turns the forearm.

layers.basics: Your biceps bends the elbow and also twists the palm up, as when you turn a screwdriver.
layers.deeper: It attaches to the shoulder blade and the radius. It is a strong supinator when the elbow is bent.
layers.expert: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5-C6); crosses both shoulder and elbow, so it is biarticular. Distal biceps tendon rupture causes a 'Popeye' bulge.

did_you_know: Its main job is actually turning the forearm, not just bending the elbow.

title: Triceps brachii
summary: The three-headed muscle at the back of the arm that straightens the elbow.

layers.basics: The triceps pushes your arm straight. It is the opposing partner of the biceps.
layers.deeper: Its long head also helps extend the shoulder.
layers.expert: Radial nerve (C6-C8); the long head originates on the infraglenoid tubercle, lateral and medial heads from the humeral shaft.

title: Rectus abdominis
summary: The paired strap muscles at the front of the abdomen that bend the trunk.

layers.basics: These are the 'six-pack' muscles; they curl your trunk forward and brace the belly.
layers.deeper: Tendinous intersections divide each muscle into segments inside the rectus sheath.
layers.expert: Innervated by thoracoabdominal nerves (T7-T12); critical for intra-abdominal pressure and trunk flexion.

did_you_know: The 'six-pack' is just these muscles divided by bands of tissue and shown when body fat is low.

title: External obliques
summary: The outermost side muscles of the abdomen that twist and bend the trunk.

layers.basics: They run diagonally along your sides and help you twist and lean.
layers.deeper: Working on one side bends and rotates to the opposite side. Both sides together flex the trunk and compress the abdomen.
layers.expert: Fibers run in a 'hands in pockets' direction; form inguinal ligament by aponeurosis. Innervated T7-T12.

did_you_know: The three layers of flat abdominal muscles run in crossing directions like plywood for strength.

title: Quadriceps femoris
summary: The four-part front thigh muscle that straightens the knee.

layers.basics: The biggest muscle on the front of your thigh, used to stand up, climb stairs and kick.
layers.deeper: Rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, medialis and intermedius share one tendon around the patella.
layers.expert: Femoral nerve (L2-L4); rectus femoris also flexes the hip. It is the largest muscle mass in the body by volume group.

did_you_know: The quadriceps tendon hosts the kneecap, the body's biggest sesamoid bone.

title: Hamstrings
summary: The three muscles at the back of the thigh that bend the knee and extend the hip.

layers.basics: These muscles pull your heel toward your buttock and help you run.
layers.deeper: Biceps femoris, semitendinosus and semimembranosus cross both hip and knee.
layers.expert: Tibial and common fibular divisions of the sciatic nerve (L5-S2); injury is common during sprinting in late swing phase.

did_you_know: The name comes from butchers hanging hams by these tendons.

title: Gastrocnemius
summary: The main calf muscle that lifts the heel.

layers.basics: The bulge of your calf; it pushes you up on tiptoe and propels each step.
layers.deeper: Its two heads join the Achilles tendon with the soleus.
layers.expert: Tibial nerve (S1-S2). The Achilles tendon stores and returns elastic energy, ~35% of running work comes from tendon recoil.

did_you_know: The Achilles tendon is the thickest and strongest tendon in the body.

title: Gluteus maximus
summary: The big buttock muscle that extends the hip.

layers.basics: The largest muscle in the body; it powers climbing, standing up and running.
layers.deeper: It extends and rotates the thigh outward and steadies the pelvis.
layers.expert: Inferior gluteal nerve (L5-S2). Insertion into the iliotibial tract and gluteal tuberosity. Its size is linked to human bipedal running.

did_you_know: Its large size is an evolutionary signature of upright walking and running.

title: Trapezius
summary: A diamond-shaped muscle across the upper back and neck that moves the shoulder blade.

layers.basics: It lets you shrug and pull your shoulder blades together.
layers.deeper: Upper, middle and lower fibers move the scapula up, back and down.
layers.expert: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) plus C3-C4. Part of the trapezius derived from branchial arch mesoderm.

did_you_know: Trapezius is named for the trapezoid shape formed by its two halves.

title: Latissimus dorsi
summary: The broad back muscle that pulls the arm down and back.

layers.basics: The widest muscle of the back, used for pulling and climbing.
layers.deeper: It runs from the lower spine and pelvis to the upper humerus, powering swimming and rowing.
layers.expert: Thoracodorsal nerve (C6-C8); also used in reconstructive flap surgery.

did_you_know: Because of its size, surgeons sometimes borrow it to rebuild other body parts.

title: Sternocleidomastoid
summary: The thick neck muscle that turns and tilts the head.

layers.basics: Look at the cords running diagonally down your neck when you turn your head; those are sternocleidomastoids.
layers.deeper: Acting on one side it tilts the head to that side and rotates the face to the other; together they flex the neck.
layers.expert: Accessory nerve (CN XI) motor, proprioception from C2-C3; congenital torticollis can result from fibrosis.

did_you_know: It also acts as a respiratory accessory muscle during heavy breathing.
